source_text: IX. Altera die post hanc visionem expectantes eramus horam illam, quando fiscalis, non cibus, sed penuria et necessitas inferretur; quia cibus nullus nobis suberat, nam et altera die ieiuni manseramus. [Sicut?] autem ut sitientibus potus, esurientibus cibus, desiderantibus martyrium obvenit, ita laboribus nostris refrigerium dominus per Lucianum carissimum nobis praebuit, qui disrupto catenarum durissimo obice, velut per duas fialas, per Herennianum hypodiaconum et Ianuarium catecuminum alimentum indeficiens omnibus ministravit. hoc subsidium aegros et laborantes nimium suffulsit: eos quoque qui per eundem laborem, hoc est per incommodum solonis et frigidae aquae, aegritudinem iam inciderant, ab infirmitate revocavit. cuius tam gloriosis operibus omnes apud deum gratias agimus.
pass_a_gloss: Literal gloss: On the next day after this vision we were awaiting that hour, when not food but a fiscal matter, indeed lack and need, would be brought in, because no food remained to us, for we had also remained fasting the other day. But just as to the thirsty drink, to the hungry food, to those longing for it martyrdom falls, so to our hardships the Lord furnished relief through our dear Lucian, who, with the hardest bar of the chains broken through, as if through two vessels, through Herennianus the subdeacon and Januarius the catechumen, supplied unfailing sustenance to all. This aid strongly upheld the sick and the weary; those also who through the same hardship, that is through the distress of solonis and of cold water, had already fallen into sickness, it recalled from weakness. For his works, so glorious, we all give thanks before God.
pass_b_english: On the day after this vision we were waiting for that hour when no meal would be brought in, but want and hardship from the imperial agent, for we had no food left, since we had remained without eating even on the day before.
Yet as drink comes to the thirsty, and food to the hungry, and martyrdom to those who desire it, so the Lord gave relief to our sufferings through our dear Lucianus.
For when the hardest bolt of our chains had been forced open, he supplied unfailing food to us all through two vessels, as it were, Herennianus the subdeacon and Januarius the catechumen.

This help bore up the sick and the exhausted exceedingly, and it drew back from infirmity even those who through that same affliction, namely the misery of the solonis and of the cold water, had already fallen ill.
For his works, so full of glory, we all give thanks before God.

choices.why: adjective used substantivally here for an official concerned with the fiscus, in context the hour of inspection or exaction rather than a meal, contrasted with cibus
fiala renders Greek phiale, a broad vessel or cup; the two men are figured as channels conveying the alms, so vessel keeps the metaphor
in prison and martyr usage it means alleviation and comfort in hardship, wider than coolness or rest alone
